note.explanation: A cell has structures that perform different jobs. The nucleus controls cell activities and contains genetic material. Organelles such as mitochondria, ribosomes, the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus and lysosomes each have special roles. In multicellular organisms, cells can become specialized to perform particular functions.
examples: Mitochondria release energy during cellular respiration.
Mesophyll cells in leaves make glucose by photosynthesis.
note.checkAnswer: Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis.
note.simple: A cell is like a small team: each part has its own job, and the parts work together.
note.checkQuestion: Which organelle is the site of protein synthesis?
note.title: Cell structures and their functions
steps: Identify the cell structure named in the question.
Recall the main job of that structure.
Connect its job to the needs of the whole cell.
note.answer: Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis.

mcqs.stem:
The process of cellular respiration occurs in:
(a) Nucleus (b) Mitochondria (c) Ribosomes (d) Golgi apparatus
rationales: The nucleus contains genetic material and controls cell activities, but is not the main site of cellular respiration.
Mitochondria are the main site of cellular respiration in eukaryotic cells.
Ribosomes make proteins rather than carrying out cellular respiration.
The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages materials rather than carrying out cellular respiration.

mcqs.stem:
The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) is primarily involved in the synthesis of:
(a) Proteins (b) Lipids (c) Carbohydrates (d) Nucleic acids
rationales: Ribosomes, especially those attached to rough ER, make proteins.
The smooth endoplasmic reticulum is primarily involved in lipid synthesis.
Carbohydrates are not the primary product of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum.
Nucleic acids are not the primary product of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum.

mcqs.stem:
Ribosomes are composed of:
(a) RNA and protein (b) DNA and protein (c) Carbohydrates and lipids (d) RNA and carbohydrates
rationales: Ribosomes are composed of ribosomal RNA and proteins.
DNA is not a structural component of ribosomes.
Carbohydrates and lipids do not make up ribosomes.
Ribosomes contain RNA, but carbohydrates are not their other main component.

mcqs.stem:
What is the primary function of ribosomes?
(a) Energy production (b) Protein synthesis (c) Lipid synthesis (d) DNA synthesis
rationales: Mitochondria are the main organelles involved in energy release by cellular respiration.
Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis.
Lipid synthesis is mainly associated with smooth endoplasmic reticulum.
DNA synthesis is not the primary function of ribosomes.

mcqs.stem:
Which cell organelle is involved in packaging and modifying proteins?
(a) Nucleus (b) Mitochondria (c) Golgi apparatus (d) Endoplasmic reticulum
rationales: The nucleus stores genetic material and controls cell activities, rather than packaging proteins.
Mitochondria release energy through cellular respiration.
The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins.
The endoplasmic reticulum helps make and transport materials, but the Golgi apparatus is the main packaging organelle.

mcqs.stem:
Which cell organelle is responsible for breaking down waste materials?
(a) Golgi apparatus (b) Nucleus (c) Mitochondria (d) Lysosome
rationales: The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages materials rather than digesting cellular waste.
The nucleus contains genetic material and controls cell activities.
Mitochondria are involved in cellular respiration, not waste digestion.
Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that break down waste materials.

mcqs.stem:
Which of the following cell structures is involved in maintaining cell shape?
(a) Cytoskeleton (b) Centrioles (c) Nucleus (d) Lysosome
rationales: The cytoskeleton supports the cell and helps maintain its shape.
Centrioles are involved in cell division in animal cells.
The nucleus contains genetic material and controls cell activities.
Lysosomes digest waste materials and do not mainly maintain cell shape.

mcqs.stem:
Which specialized region of the nucleus is responsible for ribosome assembly?
(a) Nucleoplasm (b) Nucleolus (c) Chromatin (d) Chromatin
rationales: Nucleoplasm is the fluid material inside the nucleus, not the main site of ribosome assembly.
The nucleolus is the region of the nucleus where ribosome components are assembled.
Chromatin consists mainly of DNA and proteins and is not the region responsible for ribosome assembly.
This repeated option names chromatin, which is not the region responsible for ribosome assembly.

options: Control of pH of the cell
mcqs.stem:
What is the main function of the nuclear pores?
(a) Regulation of cell division (b) Control of pH of the cell (c) Protein synthesis (d) Control of transport of molecules
rationales: Nuclear pores do not regulate cell division as their main function.
Controlling the cell's pH is not the main function of nuclear pores.
Protein synthesis occurs at ribosomes, not at nuclear pores.
Nuclear pores control the movement of molecules into and out of the nucleus.

mcqs.stem:
Which of the following cellular structures is found in animal cells and helps in cell division?
(a) Cell membrane (b) Centriole (c) Plasmodesma (d) Vacuole
rationales: A cell membrane is found in animal cells but does not perform the centriole's role in cell division.
Centrioles are found in animal cells and help in cell division.
Plasmodesmata are channels between plant cells, not animal-cell structures for division.
Vacuoles may occur in animal cells but are not the structure that helps in cell division.

mcqs.stem:
Which sub-cellular organelle plays a crucial role in energy production within the cell?
(a) Endoplasmic reticulum (b) Golgi apparatus (c) Mitochondria (d) Lysosomes
rationales: The endoplasmic reticulum makes and transports materials, rather than being the main energy-releasing organelle.
The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages materials.
Mitochondria are the main site of cellular respiration and energy release.
Lysosomes digest waste materials rather than producing energy.

mcqs.stem:
In a multicellular plant, which cell type is responsible for the production of glucose?
(a) Xylem (b) Phloem (c) Epidermal (d) Mesophyll
rationales: Xylem transports water and minerals rather than producing glucose.
Phloem transports sugars and other food substances through the plant.
Epidermal cells mainly cover and protect plant surfaces.
Mesophyll cells carry out photosynthesis and produce glucose.

mcqs.stem:
Which organelle can double its number by itself?
(a) Ribosomes (b) Lysosomes (c) Mitochondria (d) Golgi apparatus
rationales: Ribosomes make proteins, but are not the organelle identified as able to double its number by itself.
Lysosomes digest materials and do not double their number by themselves as described here.
Mitochondria can replicate and increase their number within a cell.
The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages cell products.

mcqs.stem:
Which of these are present on the surface of rough endoplasmic reticulum?
(a) Ribosomes (b) Lysosomes (c) Mitochondria (d) Vacuoles
rationales: Ribosomes are attached to the surface of rough endoplasmic reticulum.
Lysosomes are not the structures that give rough ER its rough appearance.
Mitochondria are separate organelles, not attached to rough ER as its surface structures.
Vacuoles are not the structures present on the surface of rough ER.

written.text: What are the main functions of cell membrane?
written.finalAnswer: The cell membrane encloses the cell, protects its contents and controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.

rubric.why: The answer must identify the membrane's boundary and protective role.
rubric.description: States that the membrane encloses or protects the cell.
rubric.how: Mention that it surrounds the cell and protects its contents.

rubric.why: Control of exchange is a central function of the membrane.
rubric.description: Explains that the membrane regulates movement into and out of the cell.
rubric.how: State that it controls which substances enter and leave.

modelAnswer: The cell membrane encloses the cell and protects its contents.
It controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.
The cell membrane encloses the cell, protects its contents and controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.

written.text: What key role does the Golgi apparatus play in eukaryotic cells?
written.finalAnswer: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins and other materials for transport or secretion.

rubric.why: Modification and sorting are key parts of Golgi processing.
rubric.description: Identifies processing of cell materials.
rubric.how: Say that the Golgi apparatus modifies or sorts proteins and other materials.

rubric.why: Packaging prepares materials for movement or release.
rubric.description: States that materials are packaged for transport or secretion.
rubric.how: Link packaging to transport or secretion.

modelAnswer: The Golgi apparatus modifies and sorts proteins and other materials.
It packages them for transport or secretion.
The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins and other materials for transport or secretion.

written.text: How do lysosomes contribute to the cell's functioning?
written.finalAnswer: Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that break down waste materials, worn-out cell parts and foreign substances.

rubric.why: The enzymes explain how lysosomes perform their work.
rubric.description: Mentions lysosomal digestive enzymes.
rubric.how: State that lysosomes contain enzymes that digest materials.

rubric.why: Naming what is digested explains the lysosome's role in cell maintenance.
rubric.description: Gives waste, worn-out parts or foreign substances as targets.
rubric.how: Name at least one material that lysosomes break down.

modelAnswer: Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes.
These enzymes break down waste materials, worn-out cell parts and foreign substances.
Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that break down waste materials, worn-out cell parts and foreign substances.

written.text: Which organelle detoxifies harmful substances and breaks down lipids?
written.finalAnswer: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER).

rubric.why: The question asks for the organelle, so the correct identification earns the answer marks.
rubric.description: Names the smooth endoplasmic reticulum.
rubric.how: Write smooth endoplasmic reticulum or SER.

modelAnswer: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum detoxifies harmful substances and breaks down lipids.
The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER).

written.text: What is the smooth endoplasmic reticulum responsible for?
written.finalAnswer: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum synthesizes lipids and helps detoxify harmful substances.

rubric.why: Lipid synthesis is a main SER function.
rubric.description: Identifies lipid synthesis.
rubric.how: State that SER makes or synthesizes lipids.

rubric.why: Detoxification is another important function of SER.
rubric.description: Identifies detoxification of harmful substances.
rubric.how: Mention that SER helps detoxify harmful substances.

modelAnswer: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum synthesizes lipids.
It also helps detoxify harmful substances.
The smooth endoplasmic reticulum synthesizes lipids and helps detoxify harmful substances.

written.text: How do the vacuoles in plant cells differ from vacuoles in animal cells?
written.finalAnswer: Plant cells usually have one large central vacuole containing cell sap, while animal cells usually have smaller, temporary vacuoles or may have none.

rubric.why: The large central vacuole is the main plant-cell distinction.
rubric.description: Describes the usual plant-cell vacuole.
rubric.how: State that plant cells usually have one large central vacuole.

rubric.why: A comparison must also describe animal-cell vacuoles.
rubric.description: Contrasts animal-cell vacuoles with the plant-cell vacuole.
rubric.how: Say that animal cells have smaller, temporary vacuoles or may lack them.

modelAnswer: Plant cells usually have one large central vacuole containing cell sap.
Animal cells usually have smaller, temporary vacuoles or may have none.
Plant cells usually have one large central vacuole containing cell sap, while animal cells usually have smaller, temporary vacuoles or may have none.

written.text: What could happen if lysosomal enzymes stop working properly?
written.finalAnswer: Waste and worn-out cell parts may not be digested and may accumulate, damaging the cell.

rubric.why: The answer must connect enzyme failure to failed digestion.
rubric.description: Explains that lysosomal digestion is reduced or stops.
rubric.how: State that waste or worn-out parts are no longer broken down.

rubric.why: The consequences of undigested material complete the explanation.
rubric.description: Describes accumulation or resulting cell damage.
rubric.how: Explain that undigested materials can build up and harm the cell.

modelAnswer: Waste materials and worn-out cell parts may not be digested.
They may accumulate and damage the cell.
Waste and worn-out cell parts may not be digested and may accumulate, damaging the cell.

written.text: Why are the cristae important for cellular respiration?
written.finalAnswer: Cristae increase the inner surface area of mitochondria, providing more space for the reactions of cellular respiration and energy release.

rubric.why: The folds of the cristae provide more inner mitochondrial surface.
rubric.description: States that cristae increase inner surface area.
rubric.how: Mention the increased inner surface of the mitochondrion.

rubric.why: The additional surface supports respiration reactions and energy release.
rubric.description: Connects increased surface area to respiration.
rubric.how: Explain that more surface is available for respiratory reactions.

modelAnswer: Cristae are folds that increase the inner surface area of mitochondria.
They provide more space for cellular respiration reactions and energy release.
Cristae increase the inner surface area of mitochondria, providing more space for the reactions of cellular respiration and energy release.

written.text: How are chromatin and chromosomes related?
written.finalAnswer: Chromatin is the thread-like material made of DNA and proteins; when it condenses, it forms visible chromosomes.

rubric.why: The composition of chromatin establishes what the material is.
rubric.description: Identifies chromatin as DNA associated with proteins.
rubric.how: State that chromatin consists of DNA and proteins.

rubric.why: The answer must explain how chromatin relates to chromosomes.
rubric.description: Explains that condensed chromatin forms chromosomes.
rubric.how: Describe the change in form during cell division.

modelAnswer: Chromatin is thread-like material made of DNA and proteins.
When it condenses, it forms visible chromosomes.
Chromatin is the thread-like material made of DNA and proteins; when it condenses, it forms visible chromosomes.

written.text: Which type of cell is responsible for sending nerve signals?
written.finalAnswer: A nerve cell (neuron) is responsible for sending nerve signals.

rubric.why: The question asks for the specialized cell type.
rubric.description: Names a neuron or nerve cell.
rubric.how: Write nerve cell or neuron.

modelAnswer: A nerve cell, or neuron, is responsible for sending nerve signals.
A nerve cell (neuron) is responsible for sending nerve signals.

written.text: What do mesophyll cells do in plant leaves?
written.finalAnswer: Mesophyll cells carry out photosynthesis and produce glucose.

rubric.why: Photosynthesis is the main activity of mesophyll cells.
rubric.description: Names photosynthesis as their function.
rubric.how: State that mesophyll cells carry out photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Glucose production is the outcome asked about in the chapter's cell-type context.
rubric.description: States that photosynthesis produces glucose.
rubric.how: Mention glucose as the product.

modelAnswer: Mesophyll cells carry out photosynthesis.
Photosynthesis produces glucose.
Mesophyll cells carry out photosynthesis and produce glucose.

written.text: How would you define a stem cell?
written.finalAnswer: A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell that can divide and develop into specialized cell types.

rubric.why: A stem cell is not yet committed to a specialized role.
rubric.description: Describes a stem cell as undifferentiated or unspecialized.
rubric.how: Use the term undifferentiated or explain that it is not specialized.

rubric.why: The ability to divide and form specialized cells distinguishes stem cells.
rubric.description: States its ability to divide or become specialized.
rubric.how: Mention division and development into specialized cell types.

modelAnswer: A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell.
It can divide and develop into specialized cell types.
A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell that can divide and develop into specialized cell types.

written.text:
Name the chemical compounds that make up:
(a) Cell membrane
(b) Fungal cell wall
(c) Plant cell wall
(d) Bacterial cell wall
(e) Ribosomes
(f) Chromosomes
written.finalAnswer:
(a) Lipids and proteins
(b) Chitin
(c) Cellulose
(d) Peptidoglycan (murein)
(e) RNA and proteins
(f) DNA and proteins

rubric.why: Correctly identifying the listed cell materials demonstrates knowledge of cell composition.
rubric.description: Correctly names the membrane, fungal wall and plant wall materials.
rubric.how: Give lipids and proteins, chitin, and cellulose for (a)–(c).

rubric.why: Bacterial wall, ribosome and chromosome composition complete the list.
rubric.description: Correctly names bacterial wall, ribosome and chromosome materials.
rubric.how: Give peptidoglycan, RNA and proteins, and DNA and proteins for (d)–(f).

modelAnswer: (a) Cell membrane: lipids and proteins.
(b) Fungal cell wall: chitin.
(c) Plant cell wall: cellulose.
(d) Bacterial cell wall: peptidoglycan (murein).
(e) Ribosomes: RNA and proteins.
(f) Chromosomes: DNA and proteins.
(a) Lipids and proteins; (b) chitin; (c) cellulose; (d) peptidoglycan (murein); (e) RNA and proteins; (f) DNA and proteins.

written.text: Explain the fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane.
written.finalAnswer: The fluid mosaic model describes the cell membrane as a flexible phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it. The phospholipids and many proteins can move sideways, making the membrane fluid, while the different proteins form a mosaic. The membrane is selectively permeable and controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.

rubric.why: The bilayer is the basic structural framework of the membrane.
rubric.description: Identifies the phospholipid bilayer.
rubric.how: Describe the membrane as two layers of phospholipids.

rubric.why: Embedded proteins account for the mosaic part of the model.
rubric.description: Explains the proteins in the membrane.
rubric.how: State that proteins are embedded in or associated with the bilayer.

rubric.why: Movement within the membrane accounts for its fluid nature.
rubric.description: Explains why the membrane is fluid.
rubric.how: Mention sideways movement of phospholipids or proteins.

rubric.why: The model should connect membrane structure to its exchange function.
rubric.description: States that the membrane controls passage of substances.
rubric.how: Explain that it is selectively permeable.

modelAnswer: The cell membrane consists of a flexible phospholipid bilayer.
Proteins are embedded in the bilayer and form a mosaic pattern.
Phospholipids and many proteins can move sideways, so the membrane is fluid.
The selectively permeable membrane controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.

The fluid mosaic model describes the cell membrane as a flexible phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it. The phospholipids and many proteins can move sideways, making the membrane fluid, while the different proteins form a mosaic. written.text: Describe the structure and functions of the cell wall.
written.finalAnswer: The cell wall is a rigid, non-living layer outside the cell membrane. In plants it is mainly made of cellulose; fungal walls contain chitin and bacterial walls contain peptidoglycan. It supports and protects the cell, maintains its shape and prevents it from bursting when water enters.

rubric.why: The location and basic nature describe the wall's structure.
rubric.description: Describes the wall as an outer rigid layer.
rubric.how: State that it is a rigid layer outside the cell membrane.

rubric.why: Cellulose is the main material in plant cell walls.
rubric.description: Names the material of the plant wall.
rubric.how: Identify cellulose as the plant cell-wall material.

rubric.why: Support, protection and shape are main wall functions.
rubric.description: Gives support, protection or shape maintenance.
rubric.how: Explain how the wall supports or protects the cell.

rubric.why: The wall resists internal pressure when water enters the cell.
rubric.description: Explains resistance to bursting under water pressure.
rubric.how: Mention that the rigid wall prevents the cell from bursting.

modelAnswer: The cell wall is a rigid, non-living layer outside the cell membrane.
Plant cell walls are mainly made of cellulose; fungal walls contain chitin and bacterial walls contain peptidoglycan.
The wall supports and protects the cell and helps maintain its shape.
It resists the pressure caused by water entering the cell and prevents the cell from bursting.

The cell wall is a rigid, non-living layer outside the cell membrane. In plants it is mainly made of cellulose; fungal walls contain chitin and bacterial walls contain peptidoglycan. It supports and protects the cell, maintains its shape and prevents it from bursting when water enters.

written.text: Discuss the components of the nucleus.
written.finalAnswer: The nucleus is surrounded by a double nuclear membrane containing pores. It contains nucleoplasm, chromatin and a nucleolus. The nuclear pores control transport into and out of the nucleus; chromatin contains DNA and proteins and forms chromosomes when condensed; the nucleolus assembles ribosome components.

rubric.why: The nuclear envelope and pores are key structural components.
rubric.description: Describes the nuclear membrane and pores.
rubric.how: Name the double membrane and its pores.

rubric.why: Nucleoplasm is a main component within the nucleus.
rubric.description: Names and identifies nucleoplasm.
rubric.how: Mention the fluid material inside the nucleus.

rubric.why: Chromatin carries the genetic material.
rubric.description: Explains the chromatin component.
rubric.how: State that chromatin contains DNA and proteins.

rubric.why: The nucleolus's role is an important nuclear component function.
rubric.description: Identifies the nucleolus and its role.
rubric.how: State that it assembles ribosome components.

modelAnswer: The nucleus is surrounded by a double nuclear membrane containing pores.
The pores control the movement of molecules into and out of the nucleus.
The nucleoplasm is the fluid material inside the nucleus.
Chromatin consists of DNA and proteins and condenses to form chromosomes.
The nucleolus assembles ribosome components.

The nucleus is surrounded by a double nuclear membrane containing pores. It contains nucleoplasm, chromatin and a nucleolus. The nuclear pores control transport into and out of the nucleus; chromatin contains DNA and proteins and forms chromosomes when condensed; the nucleolus assembles ribosome components.

written.text: Describe the structure and function of lysosome and endoplasmic reticulum.
written.finalAnswer: Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs containing digestive enzymes. They break down waste, foreign materials and worn-out cell parts. The endoplasmic reticulum is a network of membranes in the cytoplasm. Rough ER has ribosomes and helps synthesize and transport proteins; smooth ER has no ribosomes and synthesizes lipids and helps detoxify harmful substances.

rubric.why: Lysosome structure is needed to explain its digestive role.
rubric.description: Describes lysosomes as enzyme-containing membrane-bound sacs.
rubric.how: Name the membrane and digestive enzymes.

rubric.why: The answer must give the lysosome function.
rubric.description: States what lysosomes digest.
rubric.how: Mention waste, foreign materials or worn-out cell parts.

rubric.why: Rough ER structure and protein role are required.
rubric.description: Describes rough ER and its function.
rubric.how: State that ribosomes on rough ER help make proteins.

rubric.why: Smooth ER has distinct functions from rough ER.
rubric.description: Describes a smooth ER function.
rubric.how: Mention lipid synthesis or detoxification.

modelAnswer: Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs containing digestive enzymes.
They digest waste, foreign materials and worn-out cell parts.
The endoplasmic reticulum is a network of membranes in the cytoplasm.
Rough ER has ribosomes and helps synthesize and transport proteins.
Smooth ER has no ribosomes; it synthesizes lipids and helps detoxify harmful substances.

Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs containing digestive enzymes. They break down waste, foreign materials and worn-out cell parts. The endoplasmic reticulum is a network of membranes in the cytoplasm. Rough ER has ribosomes and helps synthesize and transport proteins; smooth ER has no ribosomes and synthesizes lipids and helps detoxify harmful substances.

written.text: Describe the formation and function of the Golgi complex.
written.finalAnswer: The Golgi complex is formed from stacks of flattened membrane-bound sacs called cisternae. It receives proteins and other materials from the endoplasmic reticulum, modifies and sorts them, and packages them into vesicles for transport or secretion.

rubric.why: The stacked sacs describe the Golgi complex's structure.
rubric.description: Describes the Golgi structure.
rubric.how: Name the flattened sacs or cisternae arranged in stacks.

rubric.why: The Golgi processes material arriving from the ER.
rubric.description: States where Golgi materials come from.
rubric.how: Mention receipt of materials from the endoplasmic reticulum.

rubric.why: Modification and sorting are central Golgi functions.
rubric.description: Explains processing of materials.
rubric.how: State that the Golgi modifies and sorts its contents.

rubric.why: Packaging completes the pathway for delivery or release.
rubric.description: Explains packaging and destination.
rubric.how: Mention vesicles for transport or secretion.

modelAnswer: The Golgi complex consists of stacks of flattened membrane-bound sacs called cisternae.
It receives proteins and other materials from the endoplasmic reticulum.
It modifies and sorts these materials.
It packages them into vesicles for transport or secretion.

written.text: Describe the structure and functions of the chloroplast.
written.finalAnswer: A chloroplast is surrounded by a double membrane and contains chlorophyll in its thylakoid membranes. Thylakoids are arranged in stacks called grana and lie in the fluid stroma. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, absorbing light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, with oxygen released.

rubric.why: The double membrane is a key structural feature.
rubric.description: Identifies the chloroplast envelope.
rubric.how: State that a chloroplast has a double membrane.

rubric.why: Chlorophyll in the membrane system captures light.
rubric.description: Describes chlorophyll and the thylakoid or grana structure.
rubric.how: Mention chlorophyll and thylakoids arranged in grana.

rubric.why: The stroma is another important structural component.
rubric.description: Names the stroma.
rubric.how: Identify the fluid region surrounding the grana.

rubric.why: The chloroplast's main function is photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Explains photosynthesis as its function.
rubric.how: State that it uses light energy to make glucose.

modelAnswer: A chloroplast is surrounded by a double membrane.
It contains chlorophyll in thylakoid membranes; thylakoids are arranged in stacks called grana.
The grana lie in the fluid stroma.
Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, using light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water and releasing oxygen.

A chloroplast is surrounded by a double membrane and contains chlorophyll in its thylakoid membranes. Thylakoids are arranged in stacks called grana and lie in the fluid stroma. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, absorbing light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, with oxygen released.

written.text: How does turgor pressure develop in a plant cell?
written.finalAnswer: Water enters a plant cell by osmosis, causing the vacuole to swell. The cell contents press against the cell wall, and the rigid wall resists this pressure; this produces turgor pressure and makes the cell firm.

rubric.why: Water entry by osmosis begins the development of turgor.
rubric.description: Identifies water entry by osmosis.
rubric.how: State that water enters the cell by osmosis.

rubric.why: The expanding vacuole increases pressure within the cell.
rubric.description: Explains the vacuole's response.
rubric.how: Mention that the vacuole swells as it takes in water.

rubric.why: Pressure against the wall is the defining physical interaction.
rubric.description: Describes the contents pressing on the wall.
rubric.how: State that the swollen contents push against the cell wall.

rubric.why: The wall's resistance gives the cell firmness.
rubric.description: Names the resulting turgor pressure and effect.
rubric.how: Explain that the wall resists expansion, making the cell turgid.

modelAnswer: Water enters a plant cell by osmosis.
The vacuole takes in water and swells.
The cell contents press against the cell wall.
The rigid cell wall resists this pressure, producing turgor pressure and making the cell firm.

Water enters a plant cell by osmosis, causing the vacuole to swell. The cell contents press against the cell wall, and the rigid wall resists this pressure; this produces turgor pressure and makes the cell firm.

written.text: Write any four differences between a plant cell and an animal cell.
written.finalAnswer: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall; animal cells do not. Plant cells contain chloroplasts; animal cells do not. Plant cells usually have one large central vacuole; animal cells usually have smaller vacuoles or none. Plant cells often have a more fixed, regular shape; animal cells usually have a more flexible, irregular shape.

rubric.why: The cell wall is a major structural difference.
rubric.description: Compares cell-wall presence.
rubric.how: State that plant cells have a cellulose wall and animal cells do not.

rubric.why: Chloroplast presence distinguishes photosynthetic plant cells from animal cells.
rubric.description: Compares chloroplast presence.
rubric.how: State that typical plant cells have chloroplasts and animal cells do not.

rubric.why: The usual vacuole sizes differ.
rubric.description: Compares vacuoles.
rubric.how: Describe the large central plant vacuole and smaller animal vacuoles.

rubric.why: Cell shape is another valid comparison.
rubric.description: Compares usual cell shapes.
rubric.how: Link a more fixed plant shape with a more flexible animal-cell shape.

rubric.why: The question explicitly asks for four differences and the response must present a clear comparison.
rubric.description: Presents four distinct paired differences clearly.
rubric.how: Use a table or paired statements and include four valid differences.

modelAnswer: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall; animal cells do not.
Plant cells contain chloroplasts; animal cells do not.
Plant cells usually have one large central vacuole; animal cells usually have smaller vacuoles or none.
Plant cells often have a more fixed, regular shape; animal cells usually have a more flexible, irregular shape.
These are four differences between plant cells and animal cells.

written.text: Describe the concept of division of labour and how it applies in multicellular organisms. Give at least three examples.
written.finalAnswer: Division of labour means that different cells, tissues and organs perform different specialized functions. This makes a multicellular organism work efficiently. For example, red blood cells transport oxygen, nerve cells carry signals, and muscle cells contract to cause movement. In plants, xylem transports water and mesophyll cells carry out photosynthesis.

rubric.why: A correct definition is needed before applying the concept.
rubric.description: Defines division of labour.
rubric.how: Explain that different parts perform different specialized jobs.

rubric.why: This explains the benefit of specialization to the organism.
rubric.description: Explains why division of labour is useful.
rubric.how: State that specialization allows the organism to work efficiently.

rubric.why: Examples must connect cell types to their functions.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of specialized cells.
rubric.how: Name a specialized cell and its role.

rubric.why: The question requires at least three examples.
rubric.description: Adds further valid examples.
rubric.how: Give two more correct cell, tissue or organ examples.

rubric.why: A third clearly stated example satisfies the minimum requested.

Division of labour means that different cells, tissues and organs perform different specialized functions. This makes a multicellular organism work efficiently. written.text: Write a note on cell specialization.
written.finalAnswer: Cell specialization is the process by which cells develop structures suited to particular functions. Specialized cells perform specific jobs in multicellular organisms, allowing division of labour. For example, nerve cells are adapted to transmit signals, red blood cells transport oxygen, and mesophyll cells carry out photosynthesis.

written.text: What impact might mitochondrial dysfunction or absence have on other organelles' ability to operate in a cell?
written.finalAnswer: Mitochondrial dysfunction or absence would reduce the cell's ATP supply. With less energy, energy-requiring processes in other organelles, such as protein synthesis at ribosomes, transport in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, and active transport at the cell membrane, would slow or stop. The cell could fail to maintain its normal activities.

written.text: What may happen if the coordination between the ribosomes and the nucleus were to fail, and why is it so important?
written.finalAnswer: If coordination between the nucleus and ribosomes failed, the ribosomes might not receive or correctly use the genetic instructions needed to make proteins. Protein synthesis could be incorrect or stop, so enzymes and structural proteins needed for cell activities would be missing or faulty. This coordination is important because the nucleus stores the instructions and ribosomes use them to make proteins.

examTips: The exercise asks direct short questions about organelle functions, cell composition and specialized cell types. For these, give the exact organelle or cell name and one precise function.
Long questions commonly ask you to describe structure and function together. Earn marks by naming the structures first, then linking each structure to its function.
For comparison questions, write paired differences such as 'plant cells have …; animal cells do not' so the comparison is clear.
For questions asking for a number of examples or differences, provide at least that many distinct, correct points.
Use key terms accurately: phospholipid bilayer, selectively permeable, cristae, nucleolus, cisternae, grana, stroma, osmosis and turgor pressure.
For Inquisitive questions, show the cause-and-effect link: mitochondrial dysfunction reduces ATP, which affects energy-requiring cell processes.

example.question: Explain the fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane.
example.answer: The cell membrane consists of a flexible phospholipid bilayer. Proteins are embedded in the bilayer and form a mosaic pattern. Phospholipids and many proteins can move sideways, so the membrane is fluid. The selectively permeable membrane controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.

explain.title: The cell membrane
explain.body: The cell membrane surrounds the cell and controls the movement of substances into and out of it. The fluid mosaic model describes a flexible phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it.

explain.title: Organelles share the cell's work
explain.body: The nucleus contains genetic material; ribosomes make proteins; rough ER helps make and transport proteins; smooth ER makes lipids and helps detoxify substances; and the Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages materials.

explain.title: Energy, digestion and support
explain.body: Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration and release energy. Cristae increase the inner surface area for respiration. Lysosomes use digestive enzymes to break down waste. The cytoskeleton helps maintain cell shape.

explain.title: Plant-cell features
explain.body: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall and usually a large central vacuole; many also have chloroplasts for photosynthesis. Water entering by osmosis causes the cell contents to press against the wall, creating turgor pressure.

explain.title: Specialization in multicellular organisms
explain.body: Different cells are adapted for different jobs. Mesophyll cells make glucose by photosynthesis, nerve cells send signals, and other specialized cells contribute to division of labour in the organism.

mistakes: Do not confuse the nucleolus, which assembles ribosome components, with chromatin, which contains DNA and proteins.
Do not say that ribosomes make lipids: ribosomes make proteins, while smooth ER is associated with lipid synthesis.
Do not confuse rough ER with smooth ER: rough ER has ribosomes; smooth ER does not.
When describing a plant cell wall, name cellulose; fungal walls contain chitin and bacterial walls contain peptidoglycan.
For a comparison, do not list features without saying which cell type has each feature.
When explaining turgor pressure, include water entering by osmosis and the cell wall resisting the pressure.
